title: UDLF Macro Schema v0.1.0
description: Universal Detection Lifecycle Format (UDLF) macro schema. A macro is a named, reusable snippet of query logic that a detection references by name via its 'requires' block. Each document holds exactly one language, because a macro is not portable: the three platforms that support the primitive at all express it differently (a Splunk macros.conf stanza expanded as text, a Sentinel savedSearches function with a functionAlias, a LogScale saved query invoked as $"name"()). A KQL equivalent of an SPL macro is therefore a separate document reusing the same 'name'; a deployer resolves a detection's requirement on (name, language). Platforms with no macro primitive (Elastic, Google SecOps, Cortex XSIAM, SentinelOne) are absent from the language enum by design — a macro that could never be materialised should not be authorable. A Splunk tuning filter is not a special case; it is an ordinary macro with an spl definition.

id.description: Unique identifier for this macro document (UUID v4). Each language variant is its own document with its own id, so a detection's 'requires' entry names the macro rather than pinning an id.

name.description: The token the macro is referenced by, both in detection logic and in a detection's 'requires' block (e.g. 'security_content_summariesonly'). Shared across the language variants of the same logical macro. The pattern is the safe intersection of all three targets — Sentinel requires a valid KQL identifier for functionAlias, which is stricter than Splunk's macro naming.

title.description: Human-readable title. Maps to Sentinel's savedSearches 'displayName' at deploy time.

description.description: What the macro does and when to use it.

created_at.description: ISO 8601 date the macro was created (YYYY-MM-DD).

language.description: Query language of this macro, and by extension the family of platforms it can be deployed to: 'spl' -> Splunk (macros.conf stanza), 'kql' -> Microsoft Sentinel (savedSearches with a functionAlias), 'cql' -> CrowdStrike NG-SIEM / Falcon LogScale (saved query called as $"name"()). Closed to these three because no other supported platform has a macro primitive.

arguments.description: Ordered parameter list, if this is a parameterised macro. Omit entirely for a zero-argument macro — for Splunk the count is load-bearing rather than cosmetic, since arity is encoded in the stanza name ('[name(2)]' and '[name]' are different macros). Substitution is positional, and the argument names must match the tokens used in 'definition' ($name$ for spl, a bare identifier for kql, ?name for cql).

name.description: Parameter name, as it appears at the substitution point in 'definition'.

type.description: Scalar type of the parameter. Required for 'kql' and forbidden elsewhere: a Sentinel function declares a typed signature ('functionParameters: argSpan: timespan') and cannot be created without it, whereas Splunk and LogScale parameters are untyped.

default.description: Default value used when the caller omits this argument. Constrained to a scalar because neither target can express a composite one: a Sentinel function default must be a scalar literal, and LogScale's ?{name=default} form substitutes text. Forbidden for 'spl' (Splunk macros have no defaults). For 'kql' the value also cannot be a computed expression such as ago(20d), which the schema cannot detect, and defaulted parameters must come after non-defaulted ones — scripts/validate-macros.py enforces that ordering.

definition.description: The macro body — the raw query text the macro expands to or evaluates as. Deploy-neutral: it carries logic only, never the surrounding platform object's mechanics (Sentinel's savedSearches 'category', the LogScale repository or view, app or index placement). Those are the deployer's concern, for the same reason a detection's schedule lives in 'deployments[].config' rather than in its logic.

changelog.description: Append-only, chronological record of notable changes. Placed last as it grows unbounded. Replaces a separate 'updated_at' — the most recent entry's date is the effective last-updated date, and each entry's 'version' ties a change to the release it shipped in.

version.description: Semantic version this change shipped in (e.g. 1.0.0).
